Every conversation that could happen with a language model–every question, misunderstanding, explanation, and unfinished argument–produces a sequence of internal states.

Could we map that landscape? Would conversations about similar things travel through neighboring regions? Would the same idea, expressed in different languages, arrive somewhere recognizably similar?

Those questions led me to build an interactive atlas of Qwen3-1.7B ’s internal representations.

Before looking at the maps, it helps to know what is being mapped. The model breaks text into tokens – words, parts of words, or punctuation. Each token selects a row from an embedding table: a learned list of numbers that supplies its starting representation.

I wanted to map thousands of conversations and see how they take shape in vector space. The vectors I’m interested in come from the residual stream, the model’s central shared workspace. The embedding table supplies its starting vectors, with one vector at each token position, and the layers read from and add to this workspace as they process the text. Taras Tsugrii’s chapter on the residual stream explains this perspective in more detail.

In Qwen3-1.7B , each position’s vector contains 2,048 numbers. Calling this a model’s “mind” is a metaphor, but the vectors are concrete: we can record them, compare them, and examine how their geometry changes with context.

I began with 100 topics and generated question-and-answer examples across English, Chinese, German, and Croatian, alongside a separate collection of coding examples. This was a small, deliberately constructed sample of a much larger possibility space.

## Inside the embedding table

Before examining a conversation, I wanted to see the model’s starting vectors. Each input token is associated with a learned row in the embedding table. Those vectors become the initial representations that the model’s layers transform.

Each point in the orange cloud below represents one token’s input embedding, projected into three dimensions. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, or punctuation. The embedding table appears here as a cloud of starting points, with no conversation order connecting them. Rotating it gives a first glimpse of their geometry.

The embedding table already encodes learned relationships between tokens. Training shapes these vectors through patterns in how tokens are used, giving the model a meaningful starting point for understanding and processing text. The layers then refine those starting representations using the context available at each position. A whole conversation contains many token states, rather than one single 2,048-number description.

## The shape of English

I started with 900 English question-and-answer examples across 100 topics, all processed by the same frozen model.

Each token begins with a learned vector from the embedding table. Qwen ’s layers update its representation using the context available at that position. I recorded the final token states and normalized their lengths so the visualization compared directions.

Whereas the orange points show each token’s starting embedding, the colored lines connect the states the model produces from those embeddings. Each token – a word, part of a word, or punctuation – is transformed from its starting vector into a final state shaped by the conversation so far. Connecting these final states in text order gives one colored path per conversation, with many conversations shown together.

To keep the comparison fair, I computed one Global PCA frame using the vocabulary embeddings and all the conversation averages. I then revealed the datasets one at a time. Adding a language to these pictures changes visibility, while the global axes stay fixed.

Across a hundred topics, the English states seemed to occupy a thin sheet. As the camera turned, a broad shape narrowed almost to an edge.

That impression survived measurement: a best-fitting plane contained approximately 99.3% of the English token states’ variation within this 3D projection .

It was tempting to interpret the sheet as evidence that the model had compressed an enormous variety of conversations into a remarkably simple surface. Before accepting that explanation, I wanted to change something more fundamental than the topic.

## Does language change the shape?

I introduced Chinese versions of the same topics and question intents, then let Qwen generate its answers independently.

The pink states appeared in a neighboring region, visibly offset from English.

The separation made an abstract question tangible. A representation can carry information about both the subject being discussed and the language used to discuss it.

If similar questions in Chinese and English occupy different regions, what does that separation represent? The idea itself? The writing system? The vocabulary and structure the model needs to produce its answer?

The geometry alone could not disentangle those possibilities. Language, script, tokenization, wording, and answer quality all changed together in this experiment.

Perhaps expecting a representation to contain “pure meaning,” cleanly detached from the form used to express it, was already an assumption I had brought to the map.

Then I added German and Croatian.

These offered a useful comparison: two more natural languages using Latin-script writing.

German and Croatian occupied the broad neighborhood of English, with substantial overlap. Chinese remained more visibly offset in this view.

The picture suggested overlapping regions with different centers and shapes. It did not establish separate language compartments throughout the model’s entire residual space.

The shapes also reflected the practical construction of the examples. Croatian responses contained many more Qwen tokens than the English responses. More token states produce more points and line segments. A larger or denser patch therefore cannot be read directly as greater knowledge or capacity.

I was beginning to distinguish the appearance of a region from the explanations I wanted to attach to it.

## Where code fits

Next came 90 Python coding examples: list processing, sorting, binary search, graph traversal, JSON, dates, matrices, recursion, and classes.

Would code form a distant island?

Code appeared in the same broad neighborhood as English and the other Latin-script datasets. Hiding the other languages makes that visual comparison easier to inspect.

That proximity was interesting, but the construction of the dataset mattered. Python uses English-like keywords alongside punctuation and operators, and each plotted example included its English question as well as its code answer.

Even “close” needed a definition. A simple distance comparison between the projected conversation averages placed the coding dataset closer to Croatian and German than to English. Being in English’s broad visual neighborhood and having English as its closest numerical neighbor were different claims.

When we call code a language, are we talking about its symbols, its structure, or its purpose? In this experiment, several of those properties were entangled in the same examples.

## Changing the window

The Global PCA fit contained 151,936 normalized input embeddings and 3,690 conversation averages . Vocabulary embeddings accounted for roughly 98% of its fitting points.

PCA does not know which observations I consider most interesting. It finds directions that explain variation in the data I give it.

So I tried Conversation PCA : choose the directions using the conversation averages alone, then project the same saved token states and embedding table into that new frame.

The relationships became visible through a different geometry. German and Croatian spread into more distinguishable regions, while substantial overlap remained.

The change was measurable. The three Conversation PCA directions captured 80.1% of the variation between conversation averages . The three Global PCA directions captured 42.4% of that same average-vector variation .

Those percentages describe conversation averages. The token paths are shown in the resulting frame, but they were not the points used to fit it.

This exposed an important choice inside the visualization: what should the map be optimized to preserve? A vocabulary-oriented frame and a conversation-oriented frame can emphasize different relationships in the same underlying representations.

## What the map leaves out

I checked the apparent flatness against all 264,571 final token states in their original 2,048-dimensional space.

The visible sheet contained almost all the variation in the 3D view, but that view left out 82.4% of the original variation . Even the best plane fitted in the full space captured only 28.7%, with a similar 28.4% on held-out topics.

At the same time, 17.6% in three directions is a substantial concentration. If variation were spread equally across all 2,048 directions, three would account for only about 0.15%. The observed share was roughly 120 times that reference.

The axes strongly tracked language, with topic structure still present after accounting for language. This connects to earlier research on language-sensitive and shared geometry in multilingual models . These measurements describe associations in this dataset and projection.

In this post, we took an exploratory look at how conversations appear in the residual vector space an LLM uses to process text. In our three-dimensional view, thousands of conversations formed thin, overlapping sheets. Different languages and code traced paths through partly shared regions, revealing a common geometric structure across the examples.

Every few months, someone points out that the world is drowning in idle compute. Your laptop idles at an office desk. Your phone spends most of its battery waiting in your pocket. Meanwhile, tech monopolies pour hundreds of billions of dollars into sprawling, water-guzzling data centers packed with high-end clusters to train and run modern language models.

The intuitive alternative is obvious: split the model up and run it across everyone’s devices.

Yet whenever people attempt decentralized AI, they run into the same brick wall. Projects like Petals and BloomBee proved you could run inference over the public internet, but they mostly approach it through pipeline parallelism—handing entire layers to individual machines.

The trouble with that strategy is the entry fee. If Layer 14 requires 8 GB or 16 GB of memory, every device with only 2 GB or 4 GB of spare RAM gets locked out. The network ends up looking like a rickety chain of modest servers rather than a truly universal computing mesh.

The real breakthrough isn’t distributing layer by layer. It is slicing within the sub-layers themselves.

## The Two Engines of a Layer

A standard Transformer block is made of two distinct computational engines: the feed-forward / MLP block and the attention mechanism.

For a visual way to picture what changes as information passes through those blocks, I explored that in The words are the shadow . Here, the question is how to split that computation across devices.

Historically, both engines demanded continuous, dense matrix multiplication across all active parameters. But recent architectural innovations—driven by frontier open models like DeepSeek-V4-Flash —have fundamentally fractured that monolithic structure.

### 1. The MLP Layer: Radical Sparsity and Granular Experts

Modern mixture-of-experts (MoE) models no longer use one monolithic MLP block per layer. They break the feed-forward step into many isolated, specialized sub-networks. In a 284-billion-parameter model, only a fraction—around 13 billion parameters—fires for any given token.

Because experts operate independently, you do not need a machine to host an entire MLP layer. You don’t even need a machine to host an entire expert:

- Expert-level sharding: A device can host a single isolated expert, or even a subset of weights within that expert’s projection matrices .

- Targeted activation: Instead of sending massive hidden states everywhere, a smart routing layer routes the token only to the specific nodes holding the experts chosen for that exact step.

- Marginal entry costs: In this proposed design, a machine with 500 MB to 1 GB of free RAM could hold a sliver of an expert matrix and only wake up when its slice is summoned. That is a target memory budget, before runtime and communication overhead.

### 2. The Attention Mechanism: Compacting the KV Cache

The second bottleneck has always been the Key-Value (KV) cache. In traditional Multi-Head Attention, as context expands, the memory needed to store attention states explodes, making long-context inference nearly impossible on distributed consumer nodes.

Recent developments have altered this equation:

- Latent compression: Techniques like Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compress key and value projections into tiny, low-rank latent vectors. In a distributed design, nodes could exchange compressed latent representations where the partition permits it.

- Adaptive attention blocks: Rather than every token attending to every previous position across the full context window, sparse attention and computation skipping reduce context connections or computation. These are separate techniques that a swarm design could combine.

- Traffic suppression: The goal is to combine state compression with cache traffic reduction , so attention work can be sharded across edge devices without saturating consumer upload speeds.

## Breaking the Data-Center Bottleneck

Conventional wisdom holds that running tensor parallelism outside of a server rack is impossible because consumer Wi-Fi latency is orders of magnitude slower than high-speed server interconnects.

That is true if you try to replicate a dense supercomputer over home broadband. It is not necessarily true if the architecture itself is built around sparsity and localization:

The comparison describes a proposed architecture, not a measured deployment. Smaller shards reduce the weight memory needed at each device; the resulting communication still has to be engineered and benchmarked.

When nodes are organized by network topology, the router dispatches tokens based on both semantic specialty and physical proximity. Adjacent expert shards can live on nodes sharing low-latency local networks, eliminating unnecessary transatlantic round-trips.

Phones, old laptops, and Raspberry Pis still need to exchange results, so network delay matters. A promising design would keep consecutive steps on nearby devices, skip unnecessary computation, and generate several tokens between network exchanges. The goal is to let each device do more useful work before it has to wait for another.

### 1. Who is Building the Decentralized Swarm? (The Protocols)

On the decentralized edge side, several major projects are building the infrastructure to host, shard, and route models dynamically across distributed devices:

- Petals (BigScience / Open-Source): This is the direct implementation of the "BitTorrent for AI" model. Built by open-source researchers, Petals lets users shard massive models across standard internet connections. Instead of one server running a 70B parameter model, Node A runs layers 1–8, Node B runs 9–16, and activations are routed peer-to-peer.

- Aethir & Akash Network: These are decentralized compute networks designed to aggregate consumer GPUs, edge nodes, and underutilized data centers into a unified global cloud. They provide the raw decentralized substrate where micro-experts can be hosted.

- Exollama / Exo: Projects emerging in the local LLM community focused on P2P cluster inference . Exo allows everyday users to link laptops, phones, and desktop GPUs over local Wi-Fi or peer networks to run unified split-model inference without relying on cloud APIs.

### 2. Who is Building the Architecture? (The Frontier Labs)

While decentralized protocols build the network , traditional frontier labs are building the sparse geometric mathematics (MoE, compressed cache, dynamic depth) to run internally on their hardware:

- DeepSeek: They have proven to be the most aggressive innovators in KV cache compression . Their introduction of Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) —which compresses historical tokens into low-rank latent vectors—is the exact mathematical mechanism required to run high-context models on limited edge memory.

- OpenAI (Noam Shazeer & Architecture Research): Shazeer (who invented MoE and co-invented the Transformer) leads next-generation architecture research. His focus centers on breaking away from rigid Transformer stacks toward dynamic-depth, continuous execution, and non-standard architectures like State-Space Models (SSMs).

- Google DeepMind: They pioneered Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) , proving mechanically that you can route tokens down variable vertical paths while preserving fixed GPU batching shapes using top- k capacity routing.

### 3. Why This Could Be Massive (The Market Shift)

This architecture isn't just an interesting engineering trick; it fundamentally restructures the economics of AI:

- Destruction of the Cloud API Monopoly: Today, AI intelligence is tied to cloud subscriptions controlled by a handful of centralized data center owners. An efficient, decentralized edge-swarm protocol bypasses compute monopolies completely, democratizing frontier-level intelligence.

- Unlocking Edge NPUs: Millions of modern smartphones, laptops, and local devices ship with integrated Neural Processing Units (NPUs) that sit mostly idle. A peer-to-peer routing network transforms that global, dormant consumer hardware into the largest supercomputer on Earth.

- Zero-Trust Privacy: If processing takes place across local micro-experts and compressed latent shadows, sensitive data never has to be reconstructed into plain text on a centralized corporate server.

Whoever successfully connects these two halves— the sparse dynamic geometry (MoE + compressed KV + dynamic paths) with the decentralized protocol layer (P2P routing)—will own the post-cloud infrastructure of intelligence.

## The Democratization of Compute

For the last decade, AI progress has favored centralization: bigger clusters, higher thermal envelopes, and deeper corporate pockets.

Building a swarm on sub-layer sharding inverts that incentive structure. Millions of office laptops, phones, smart TVs, and retired hardware—previously dismissed as e-waste in the LLM era—could become functional cells in an emergent supercomputer.

The path forward won’t come from waiting for consumer home internet to mimic data center fiber. It will come from software that treats sparsity, adaptive attention, and sub-layer fragmentation as native design principles. When models can be sliced thin enough to fit anywhere, intelligence stops belonging exclusively to the companies that own the data centers.

An architectural argument based on the linked research. The proposed swarm, tiny-device memory budgets, and end-to-end network efficiency have not been demonstrated here.
